Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.diiq.gov.ph OILG OPINtON NO 08 THE HONORABLE MEMBERS OF THE SANGGUNIANG PANLALAWIGAN OF LOCOS NORTE Thru: HON. CECILIA ARANETA-MARCOS Vice-Governor and Presiding Officer Provincial Capitol, Laoag City Gentlemen/Ladies: This refers to the earlier letter from Mr. Alan Melquiades A. Agustin, Secretary to the Sanggunian, Sangguniang Panlungsod, Laoag City, requesting this Department's legal opinion concerning City Ordinance No. 2023-008, Series of 2023, entitled, "An Ordinance Providing Incentive to Laoag City Registered Business Entities Employing Resident Senior Citizens and/or Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) — LaoagPWDe", which was declared invalid by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Ilocos Norte. As culled from the attached Privilege Speech of Sangguniang Panlungsod (SP) Member John Michael V. Farinas—who sponsored the aforesaid Ordinance, during the Question and Privilege Hour of the 49th Regular Session of the 12th Sangguniang Panlungsod of the City of Laoag on July 14, 2023—and its attachments, the subject ordinance was crafted with the end goal of finally creating a solution to the existing unemployment problems of qualified and Laoagueho Senior Citizens and PWDs. However, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Ilocos Norte, through its Committee on Laws as well as the Committee on Senior Citizens, declared the subject Ordinance invalid for the following reasons: 1. Section 5 of the subject ordinance lacks some of the qualifications for deduction of business tax provided under RA 7277 (Magna Carta for PWDs), as amended, and RA 9994 (Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010). 2. The superfluity and inconsistency between existing national laws and the ordinance. 3. There are two separate incentives that business entities may avail of—one from the existing laws and another from the subject ordinance. In his defense, SP member Farinas, in his privilege speech, manifested that Section 5 of the subject ordinance enumerates five (5) qualifications for deduction of business taxes. Further, he underscores, citing Section 4 of the subject Ordinance, that it is not only the qualifications in Section 5 that must be complied with but also all other conditions and guidelines explicitly stated by RA 9994 and RA 7277 and their IRRs. "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

Accordingly, the qualifications under Section 5 are guidelines for Laoagueho business entities to follow and a basis for the implementing offices concerned. As to the second observation that there exists superfluity and inconsistency between existing national laws and ordinances, SP Member Farihas countered it, claiming that the subject ordinance was enacted primarily to "localize" the application of the two laws (i.e., RA 9994 and 7277), and such being the case, there can never be an instance that a business establishment can claim two separate incentives using two separate laws— one from the ordinance and one from a national law. Hence, the subject request of Mr. Agustin. At the outset, it is to be emphasized that this Department is an agency under the executive branch of the government, and as such, it is devoid of authority to declare invalid or illegal executive or legislative measures approved by local government officials, nor does it have authority to declare invalid or illegal any acts committed by local government officials that are alleged to be in violation of the Local Government Code (hereinafter referred to as the Code) or any other applicable laws. The same must be threshed out in the proper forum. Notwithstanding, for purposes of academic discussion coupled with our objective to guide the parties concerned pursuant to the DILG Secretary's delegated general supervisory authority over local government units and their officials, we shall herein discuss the provisions of law that we deem applicable to the subject issue. While this Department is of the view that LGUs may implement national laws sans enacting ordinances, LGUs are also not precluded from enacting an ordinance for the purpose of 'localizing' a national law with the end in view of implementing such a national law. As to the extent of the review power of Sangguniang Panlalawigan vis-å-vis city/municipal ordinances, we find Section 56 (c) of the Local Government Code of 1991 (hereinafter referred to as the Code) instructive, thus: "Section 56. Review of Component City and Municipal Ordinances or Resolutions by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan. (c) If the sangguniang panlalawigan finds that such an ordinance or resolution is beyond the power conferred upon the sangguniang panlungsod or sangguniang bayan concerned, it shall declare such ordinance or resolution invalid in whole or in part. The sangguniang panlalawigan shall enter its action in the minutes and shall advise the corresponding city or municipal authorities of the action it has taken.' As can be clearly gathered from the aforequoted provision, the only ground to declare an ordinance invalid—in whole or in part—by the Sangguniang Panalalawigan is when the same is beyond the power conferred upon the sangguniang panlungsod. We find our opinion in DILG Legal Opinion No. 23, Series of 2013, pertinent to the issue at hand, and the same is worth quoting at length, thus: "xxx aside from the fact that the sangguniang panlalawigan is bound to limit its review of the appropriation ordinance to the requirements set forth by the Page 2 of 4

aforementioned provisions of the Code, Section 56 (c) thereof is clear in providing for the only ground upon which a city ordinance or resolution may be declared invalid by the sangguniang panlalawigan i.e., the ordinance is beyond the power conferred upon the sanggunian concerned. In relation thereto, the case of Moday vs. CA (G.R. No. 107916, 20 February 1997) is instructive. In the said case, the Supreme Court, citing Velasco vs. Blas (G.R No. L-30456, 20 July 1982) ruled that: 'The only group upon which a provincial board may declare any municipal resolution, ordinance, or order invalid is when such resolution, ordinance or order is 'beyond the power conferred upon the council or president making the same'. Absolutely, no other is recognized by the law. A strictly legal question is before the provincial board in its consideration of a municipal resolution, ordinance or order. The provincial (board's) disapproval of any resolution, ordinance or order must be premised specifically upon the fact that such resolution, ordinance, or order is outside the scope of the legal powers conferred by law. If a provincial board passes these limits, it usurps the legislative functions of the municipal council, or president. Such has been consistent course of executive authority." Premised from the foregoing and based on the representations in the subject letter, while it may be argued that the grounds upon which the Sangguniang Panlalawigan cited for declaring the subject ordinance invalid appear to be within its power at face value, such grounds, are untenable. It is for this reason that we are writing your good Office to re-evaluate the Sangguniang Panlalawigan's declaration as to the invalidity of the ordinance taking into account the following points: Firstly, regarding its observation that the subject ordinance lacks some of the qualifications for deduction of business tax provided under RA 7277 and RA 9994, it is to be noted that Section 4 of the subject ordinance provides a caveat that reads "xxx provided, that the qualifications and guidelines set forth by RA 9994 and RA 7277 as amended and its Implementing Rules and Regulations [and] in the immediately subsequent section are complied." Verily, well-settled is the rule in statutory construction that statutes must be read in their entirety. Secondly, as to the issue of superfluity and inconsistency between the subject ordinance and existing national laws, as has been established, the enactment of the subject ordinance was merely to localize RA 7277 and RA 9994. To reiterate our position, while this Department opines that LGUs may implement national laws sans enacting ordinances, LGUs are also not precluded from enacting ordinances for the purpose of localizing a national law with the end in view of fully implementing the same. And finally, anent the issue that there will be two (2) separate incentives that business entities may avail of in light of the enactment of the subject ordinance—one from the existing laws and another from the subject ordinance—we concur with the position of SP member Farinas that since the subject ordinance is merely localizing the application of the aforesaid national laws, there should be no 'double' incentives. On a final note, should there be relevant facts which were not represented in the letter of Mr. Agustin which you deem should be considered in our discussion above, we will be glad to hear from you or the august body the soonest. Thank you. Very truly yours, By the Authority of the Secretary: ATTY. JUAN VICTOR R. LLAMAS Undersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSELLAJJVULLLS-LRALLD,rjam/ClP Dir.
